summary: Lists requirements for Path Computation Clients and Path Computation Elements to support point-to-multipoint MPLS-TE paths. PCEs compute paths for traffic engineering in MPLS and GMPLS networks. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A path computation element is a separate machine that works out routes for an MPLS network so that the routers themselves do not have to. This memo says what the client asking for a route and the machine computing it must exchange when the route has one starting point and many end points.

questions: what is a pce in mpls
subtitle: What a path-computation client and a path-computation element must say to each other to plan one-to-many MPLS traffic-engineered paths.

tldr.problem: A path computation element can plan routes for an MPLS network, but the generic requirements for talking to one do not cover a tree of paths with many destinations.
tldr.mechanism: This memo lists 15 numbered requirements for the PCC-PCE protocol, covering an explicit P2MP marker, several destinations in one request, compressed or per-leaf path replies, exchanges split over several messages, branch-node limits and reoptimization thresholds.
tldr.outcome: The requirements add parameters to the messages that already exist rather than defining new ones, so they complement the generic requirements in RFC 4657 instead of replacing them.

today: RFC 5862 is an Informational memo from June 2010, and the unit metadata records no RFC that obsoletes it and none that updates it. It is not a protocol specification. It states the requirements a later PCC-PCE protocol specification can meet, and it leaves the signalling itself to other documents.

sections.title: Why Point-to-Multipoint Paths Need Their Own Requirements
sections.content:
A Path Computation Element (PCE), defined in RFC 4655, is an entity that computes a network path or route from a network graph, applying computational constraints. The plan is to use it to compute the path of traffic-engineered label switched paths (TE LSPs) in Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) and Generalized MPLS (GMPLS) networks.

A point-to-multipoint (P2MP) TE LSP is a tree of paths: it starts at one router and ends at several. The signalling requirements for such paths are in RFC 4461 and the signalling extensions are in RFC 4875. Computing such a path is a significant challenge, and optimising several of them at once needs considerable computational resources. A PCE offers a way to move that work off the label switching routers (LSRs) and onto one machine.

This memo adds to the generic PCC-PCE communication protocol requirements in RFC 4657. It does not try to justify using a PCE for P2MP traffic engineering; the applicability of the PCE-based architecture to P2MP MPLS TE is covered in the companion document RFC 5671.
sections.plainLanguage: A path computation element is a machine that works out routes for an MPLS network, so the routers themselves do not have to. This memo explains what the two sides of that conversation must say when one route has a single start and many ends.

sections.title: Requests, Replies and Multiple Destinations
sections.content:
The protocol MUST allow requests and replies for computing paths of P2MP LSPs. No new messages are needed for this, but new parameters must be added to the existing PCC-PCE messages.

An explicit parameter SHOULD be placed in a conspicuous place in the Path Computation Request so that a receiving PCE can easily tell the request is for a P2MP path (R1). A protocol specification MAY instead let an implementation infer this from the presence of certain parameters, such as a list of more than one destination, but the explicit marker is preferred. Objective functions, the criteria a PCE applies while computing, keep the requirement already stated in RFC 4657, though new objective functions specific to P2MP computation will need codepoints allocated in a separate document (R2).

PCEs are not required to support P2MP path computation, so a PCE MUST be able to reject a P2MP request with a reason code that says P2MP is not supported (R3). Early PCE implementations may lack that support and may not recognise the new parameter at all. At least one parameter required in a P2MP request MUST therefore be defined so that such a back-level PCE rejects the message automatically as unprocessable or unrecognized, with no change to that PCE (R4). The recommended choice is the explicit P2MP parameter from R1.

Because a P2MP LSP has more than one destination, a single Path Computation Request MUST be able to list several destinations (R5). The response MUST be able to carry the path of a P2MP LSP, either as a compressed path or as a non-compressed path made of a series of source-to-leaf point-to-point paths, known as S2L sub-paths (R6). By default the path returned SHOULD use the compressed format, and the request MAY state a preference for either format (R7). A single P2MP LSP can have many destinations and a very extensive tree, so a single request or response MUST be able to be carried by a sequence of PCE messages (R8); RFC 4657 already requires reliable and in-order delivery, so the parts of the sequence arrive in order and none is missing.
sections.plainLanguage: A request for a one-to-many path names every end point, and the reply can describe the tree either as a compressed set of routes or as one path per end point. The compressed form is the default. A request that a planning machine cannot handle must be refused with a clear reason, and it must also fail safely on older planning machines that have never heard of one-to-many paths.

sections.title: Changing Paths, Reoptimizing and Adding Destinations
sections.content:
All branches of a single P2MP LSP must have the same characteristics, and RFC 4875 achieves this by not allowing signalling parameters to vary per branch. It MUST NOT be possible to set different constraints, traffic parameters or quality-of-service requirements for different destinations of a P2MP LSP within a single computation request (R9).

The requirements for path modification and path diversity from RFC 4657 are unchanged, with one addition: it MUST be possible to supply an existing path in a Path Computation Request, and that path MUST be able to be a P2MP path, supplied by the PCC as a compressed path or as a non-compressed path (R10).

Reoptimization MUST be supported for P2MP TE LSPs, and the existing path MUST be supplied with the request so the PCE can do it (R11). Because P2MP LSPs are more complex, small improvements are often possible after network resources change. But re-signalling any LSP risks the stability of the service and of the network, even with make-before-break (RFC 3209). A P2MP Path Computation Request SHOULD therefore carry a parameter that lets the PCC state a cost-benefit reoptimization threshold, for the whole LSP and per destination. The setting of that parameter is subject to local policy at the PCC and SHOULD be subject to policy at the PCE, as described in RFC 5394. The response SHOULD say which of the routes have been modified from the paths supplied in the request.

Adding or removing destinations is a variation of path modification (R12). When a destination is added, a path must be computed for the new branch. The request MAY indicate the path of the existing P2MP LSP, which destinations are new additions to the tree, and which destinations of the existing tree must not have their paths modified. It MAY also carry a cost-benefit reoptimization threshold, so that adding leaves does not reoptimize the existing tree unless a certain improvement is made over grafting the new leaves on. When destinations are deleted, no new path has to be computed, although recomputing can yield better results than pruning the tree, and the full previous path of the whole P2MP TE LSP MAY be supplied.

For administrative, security or other policy reasons it may be desirable to limit which nodes can act as branch points. The PCC MUST be able to give a list of nodes that forms a limiting superset of the branch nodes, and a list of nodes that must not be used as branch nodes (R13). Finally, because only parts of a tree may need to be diverse, the PCC SHOULD be able to request a secondary P2MP path tree with partial path diversity for specific leaves or a specific S2L sub-path (R15).
sections.plainLanguage: Every branch of one tree must carry the same traffic requirements, so a single request cannot ask for different quality on different end points. To change a tree, the client sends the current path with the request and sets a threshold for how much improvement is worth re-signalling, and it can say which end points must stay as they are.

sections.title: Capabilities, Policy and Monitoring
sections.content:
The ability to perform P2MP path computation, and the objective functions a PCE supports, SHOULD be advertised as part of PCE discovery (RFC 4674). If that ability is not advertised, the protocol MUST still allow a PCC to discover which of the PCEs it talks to support P2MP computation and which P2MP objective functions each one supports (R14).

A PCE implementation MAY offer a configuration switch that enables or disables P2MP MPLS TE computations, and a change in the level of support SHOULD be re-advertised. Support and advertisement of support MAY be subject to policy: a PCE MAY hide its P2MP capabilities from certain PCCs by not advertising them and not reporting them in any capability exchange, and it MAY be directed by policy to refuse a P2MP computation for any reason, including the identity of the PCC making the request.

Protocol extensions SHOULD be accompanied by MIB objects for the control and monitoring of the protocol and of the PCE that performs the computations, either in the same MIB module used for general PCECP control and monitoring or in a new one. Those objects SHOULD allow the control and monitoring of all aspects of the protocol relevant to P2MP path computation. The liveness detection and monitoring requirements of RFC 4657 need no change, but P2MP computations are likely to take longer than point-to-point ones, and the monitoring SHOULD take that into account.

There are no extra requirements for verifying that the protocol works correctly. Verifying the PCE and its algorithms is out of scope for protocol requirements, but a PCC MAY send the same request to more than one PCE and compare the results.

A PCE works on a topology graph, which may be built from information distributed by traffic engineering extensions to the network's routing protocol. So that the PCE can select a path the signalling protocol can use to install the P2MP LSP, that graph MUST include information about the P2MP signalling and branching capabilities of each LSR in the network. If the traffic engineering extensions to the routing protocol are used, they SHOULD be as described in RFC 5073.

Using a PCE for P2MP paths is not expected to have significant impact on network operations. Adding P2MP support to a PCE that already computes point-to-point paths might, however, change the loading of that PCE significantly, and that might affect network behaviour, especially during recovery periods immediately after a network failure.
sections.plainLanguage: A planning machine should say up front that it can handle one-to-many paths, and an operator may hide that ability from some clients. The machine also needs a graph of the network that says which routers can act as branch points, or it cannot build a tree the signalling protocol can install.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
P2MP computation requests do not raise any additional security issues for the PCC-PCE communication protocol, because no new messages and no new PCC-PCE relationships or transactions are introduced.

The cost of the requests does go up. P2MP computation requests are more CPU-intensive and also use more link bandwidth. If the protocol was already susceptible to denial of service attacks based on injecting spurious Path Computation Requests, supporting P2MP path computation would make the effect worse. It would be possible to consider applying different authorization policies for P2MP Path Computation Requests compared to other requests.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing new is exposed to attackers, because the messages between the client and the planning machine stay the same. But a one-to-many request takes more work and more bandwidth, so an attacker who floods the planner with fake requests costs more each time.

items.title: Explicit P2MP marker
items.text: A parameter in a conspicuous place that says the request is for a one-to-many path.

items.title: Several destinations
items.text: One request can name every end point of the tree.

items.title: One set of constraints
items.text: Different destinations cannot get different constraints or quality-of-service requirements.

items.title: Existing path supplied
items.text: The current path travels with the request so it can be modified or reoptimized.

items.title: Reoptimization threshold
items.text: A cost-benefit threshold for the whole LSP and per destination.

items.title: Branch node lists
items.text: A limiting list of nodes that may branch, and a list that must not.
